name: Repository & Project Structure
description: Monorepo vs polyrepo, layering, dependency direction, package management and project layout that survives growth.

modules.name: Repositories
modules.description: How to organise code across teams and services.

cards.answer: A monorepo holds many projects in one repository with one history; a polyrepo gives each project its own repository and lifecycle.

left.title: Monorepo
points: One version of every internal dependency
Needs build tooling that scales (Nx, Turborepo, Bazel)

right.title: Polyrepo
points: Small, fast clones and simple CI

cards.explanation: The deciding question is how often changes cross project boundaries. Frequent cross-cutting change favours a monorepo; genuinely independent products with different release cadences favour polyrepo. A monorepo without task caching and affected-project detection becomes painfully slow.

cards.prompt: What does a monorepo need from its tooling?
cards.answer: A project graph, affected-target detection so CI only builds what changed, remote build caching, consistent task running, and code ownership rules per directory.
cards.explanation: Without affected-detection, every PR runs every test and CI time grows with the repo. Nx and Turborepo provide this for JS/TS; Bazel and Pants for polyglot repos. CODEOWNERS keeps review load routed to the right people.

cards.prompt: What do the three parts of a semantic version mean, and what do `^` and `~` allow?
cards.answer: MAJOR breaking, MINOR backwards-compatible feature, PATCH backwards-compatible fix. `^1.2.3` allows any 1.x.y at or above 1.2.3; `~1.2.3` allows 1.2.x only. Below 1.0.0 the rules are looser and `^0.2.3` allows only 0.2.x.
cards.explanation: Semver is a promise made by humans, so lockfiles exist because the promise is sometimes broken. Commit the lockfile for applications; libraries publish ranges. `npm ci` installs the lockfile exactly — that is the command CI should run.

cards.prompt: The build works locally and fails in CI with a different library version. What is the cause and the fix?
cards.answer: A lockfile that was not committed, ignored, or bypassed by an install command that resolves ranges afresh. Commit it and use the reproducible install command (`npm ci`, `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, `poetry install`).
cards.explanation: Lockfiles pin the entire transitive tree with integrity hashes — reproducibility and supply-chain protection in one file. A lockfile diff in a pull request is also a genuine review artefact: it shows exactly which new code you are about to ship.

modules.name: Code Organisation
modules.description: Layering, dependency direction and structure inside a project.

cards.prompt: What is layered architecture, and what is the one rule that makes it work?
cards.answer: Presentation → application → domain → infrastructure, with dependencies pointing in one direction only. Domain logic must not import infrastructure.
cards.explanation: One-way dependencies mean you can test the domain without a database, and swap infrastructure without touching business rules. The direction is enforced by inverting interfaces: the domain declares a repository interface, infrastructure implements it.

cards.prompt: Organising by type vs organising by feature
cards.answer: By type groups all controllers, all models, all services; by feature groups everything for one capability together.

right.title: By feature
points: A change lives in one folder
Deleting a feature is deleting a directory
Boundaries are visible in the tree
Shared code needs a deliberate home

cards.explanation: Feature folders scale better because the unit of change is a feature, not a layer. Keep a `shared`/`common` area but police it — everything drifts there by default, and a shared folder that imports from features has inverted the dependency.

cards.prompt: Why are circular imports a design smell, not just a runtime annoyance?
cards.code:
# user.py
from order import Order

# order.py
from user import User   # ImportError / partially initialised module
cards.answer: The two modules are one unit that cannot be understood, tested or reused separately. Fixes: extract the shared piece into a third module, invert one direction with an interface, or merge them if they really are one concept.
cards.explanation: At runtime the symptoms vary by language — Python raises or gives half-initialised modules, JavaScript yields undefined bindings, C++ needs forward declarations. The design problem is the same everywhere, and tools such as madge or import-linter can fail the build on cycles.

cards.prompt: What belongs in a repository's README and supporting docs?
cards.answer: What the project is in one sentence, how to run it locally, how to run the tests, how to deploy, the architecture in a diagram or a paragraph, and where to get help. Longer material goes in `docs/`, with decisions recorded as ADRs.
cards.explanation: The test is whether a new joiner can get it running without asking anyone. Architecture Decision Records are the highest-value habit here: a short dated file per significant decision, stating context, decision and consequences — it answers 'why is this like this?' years later.
